bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is yield and reproducibility: no proven batch process exists that can create multiple reliable, surface-stable junction/device regions on a single semiconductor substrate, and until such a process emerges, all routes remain dominated by device-to-device variation, contamination-driven instability, and manual-fabrication cost that prevents scaling to complex systems.

routes.route: improve point-contact devices and scale assembly of packaged transistors
routes.reason: Point-contact devices are fundamentally delicate and irreproducible, with wire-wisker contacts that drift and contaminate; scaling assembly of them multiplies failure points, and the evidence already shows junction devices are more robust, so this route cannot become a platform.

routes.route: focus on reproducible junction transistors while keeping circuit assembly discrete
routes.reason: Junction transistors are the most credible robust single device and buy time: they let systems improve while surface-stability and batch-processing research proceeds. But keeping assembly discrete limits the size/reliability payoff and alone does not solve wiring burdens, so it is a hedge, not the end goal.

routes.route: build hybrid modules that combine several separately fabricated components in one package
routes.reason: Hybrids reduce interconnection failure points and can serve military/space buyers who tolerate cost, but they depend on reliable junction devices and modest packaging; they are a pragmatic intermediate but do not attack the core reproducibility/batch-process frontier, so fund only as a stopgap.

routes.route: search for a surface-protection and patterned batch process that can create multiple junction/device regions reproducibly on one semiconductor substrate
routes.reason: This is the only route that addresses the root bottleneck: reproducibility, surface stability, and interconnection burdens simultaneously. Photographic masking plus diffusion plus a passivating surface layer is the highest-information bet, as it directly tests whether the solid-state effect becomes a batch platform.

routes.route: abandon monolithic integration as unnecessary until discrete transistors become much cheaper
routes.reason: Deferring integration surrenders the size, power, and reliability advantages that the pressure explicitly demands, and discrete wiring burdens are shown to multiply failure and assembly cost; waiting is a negative-position strategy with no evidence that discrete costs will collapse.

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is that ocean-floor observations are sparse, expensive, and indirect, so no single dataset yet cleanly discriminates mobile-ocean-floor (seafloor-spreading) predictions from flexible fixed-crust reinterpretations; the challenge is to design tests with strong a priori discriminating power before committing to a global synthesis.

routes.route: continue accumulating regional geology without committing to horizontal ocean-floor motion
routes.reason: It does not carve nature at the joints: accumulation without a discriminating hypothesis cannot decide between moving-floor and fixed-crust alternatives, and the structured mid-ocean ridge system and magnetic anomalies are crying out for a mechanism-driven test.

routes.route: test seafloor spreading by predicting systematic age/magnetic patterns on both sides of ridges
routes.reason: This is the highest-information and most falsifiable route: if spreading is real, magnetic anomaly sequences and crustal ages should be symmetric and increasingly old away from each ridge; a clean confirmation or refutation discriminates against post-hoc fixed-crust explanations.

routes.route: focus on mantle-convection mechanisms before treating ocean-floor geometry as decisive
routes.reason: Mechanism work is a worthy complement but cannot alone arbitrate between mobile and fixed crust; without first locking down the kinematic prediction (ages/patterns), convection arguments remain theory-laden and insufficiently grounded in the new oceanographic data.

routes.route: map earthquake geometry around ridges/trenches/offset faults to test coherent moving boundaries
routes.reason: Earthquake mechanism and relocated epicenter patterns along fracture zones and trenches are a genuine independent check of coherent moving boundaries, and seismology is relatively cheap compared to direct seafloor sampling; it can corroborate or undermine the spreading geometry.

routes.route: treat the ridge and magnetic anomalies as unrelated until direct crustal ages are available
routes.reason: This refuses the central opportunity: the structural and magnetic data are the best currently available proxies for crustal history, and waiting indefinitely for costly direct ages forfeits the discriminating power already latent in the anomaly symmetry prediction.

bet.topRoute: test seafloor spreading by predicting systematic age/magnetic patterns on both sides of ridges
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Collect continuous magnetic anomaly profiles across several ridge segments and test whether the anomaly sequences are mirror-symmetric about the axis and whether pattern spacing scales consistently with distance from the ridge, using the continental paleomagnetic reversal chronology to generate quantitative age-versus-distance predictions rather than post-hoc pattern matching.
requiredComplements: kinematic prediction of linear age gradient away from ridge axes
continental paleomagnetic reversal timescale as a quantitative clock
relocated earthquake epicenters along fracture zones showing ridge-transform offsets
heat-flow profiles trending high at ridges and decreasing with distance
direct crustal age sampling at a few key symmetric locations for calibration
sediment thickness profiles as an independent proxy for crustal age
mainFailureRisks: magnetic anomalies may be dominated by source geometry/intensity variations rather than polarity reversals, breaking the symmetry prediction
reversal chronology on continents may be too coarse or uncertain to provide a quantitative clock, leaving rates unconstrained
ocean-floor access costs may limit sampling to too few ridge transects to distinguish symmetry from coincidence
a high degree of unexplained asymmetry in anomaly patterns could force ad-hoc amendments, weakening the discriminating test
mantle-convection advocates may reject kinematic evidence as insufficient to settle mechanism, stalling synthesis
bet.generalizationBoundary: The symmetry/age-gradient prediction applies to stable mid-ocean ridge segments with approximately symmetric spreading; it does not automatically transfer to asymmetric spreading zones, ridge jumps, trenches where crust is consumed, transform boundaries, or continental rift margins unless their kinematics are independently constrained by the same quantitative framework.
unresolvedUnknowns: reversal rate and duration statistics across the geological past
whether anomaly amplitude variation tracks source intensity changes vs. polarity state
actual spreading rate magnitudes needed to match chronicle timelines
role of transform faults in preserving or distorting symmetric anomaly records
whether heat-flow and sediment proxies track the same age gradient in all basins

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is that ocean-floor observations remain sparse, expensive, and indirect: heat flow, sediment thickness, magnetism, and earthquake locations each individually admit flexible fixed-crust (contracting-earth or vertical-evolution) interpretations, so no single dataset yet discriminates seafloor spreading from static alternatives. The value of predictions depends on converting the vague spreading idea into specific testable patterns (systematic bilateral symmetry of age, magnetic anomaly sequence, and sediment thickness) that a fixed-crust account cannot mimic without ad hoc assumptions.

routes.route: continue accumulating regional geology without committing to horizontal ocean-floor motion
routes.reason: Regional accumulation is necessary context but does not actively discriminate mobile-floor from fixed-crust models; it is low-cost insurance but should be subordinated to tests that can actually falsify or support spreading given sparse access.

routes.route: test seafloor spreading by predicting systematic age/magnetic patterns on both sides of ridges
routes.reason: This is the cheapest decisive test available: if the ridge creates new crust that splits symmetrically, then magnetic anomaly sequences, age, sediment thickness, and bathymetric depth should be symmetric about the ridge axis; a fixed-crust model has no reason to predict such bilateral symmetry, so this discriminates strongly.

routes.route: focus on mantle-convection mechanisms before treating ocean-floor geometry as decisive
routes.reason: Mechanism studies are scientifically important but cannot adjudicate whether motion actually happens; geometry and pattern tests should come first because they can falsify motion outright, and a mechanism only gains urgency after kinematic evidence looks real.

routes.route: map earthquake geometry around ridges/trenches/offset faults to test coherent moving boundaries
routes.reason: Earthquake geometry provides an independent, relatively coarse-grained check on whether ridges, trenches, and transform/offset faults act as coherent kinematically linked boundaries; this complements but does not substitute for the symmetric-pattern test because precise epicenter coverage is incomplete.

routes.route: treat the ridge and magnetic anomalies as unrelated until direct crustal ages are available
routes.reason: Waiting for direct crustal ages is the most expensive and slowest route given sparse drilling access, and the magnetic anomaly record is already the highest-resolution geometric signal available; ignoring the ridge-anomaly linkage wastes the most informative data currently in hand.

bet.topRoute: test seafloor spreading by predicting systematic age/magnetic patterns on both sides of ridges
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: On a well-surveyed ridge segment with a long magnetic profile crossing the axis, take the observed sequence of linear magnetic anomalies and test whether the sequence and spacing are mirror-symmetric about the ridge axis, and whether the anomaly spacing is proportional to distance from the axis under a constant-reversal chronology derived from the independently established continental paleomagnetic reversal record; if fixed-crust accounts can only reproduce this by positing distinct ad hoc crustal histories on each flank, the symmetry/fit stands as decisive support for spreading.
requiredComplements: symmetry analysis of sediment thickness vs. distance from ridge axis
bathymetric depth vs. crustal age relationship across flanks
transform/offset fault earthquake relocation to confirm coherent fracture zones
reversal chronology transfer from continental paleomagnetic columns to ocean anomaly sequences
heat-flow decay profile away from ridge crest as a cooling-scale check
mainFailureRisks: asymmetric spreading or non-constant rates could smear the predicted mirror symmetry and delay rejection of fixed-crust alternatives
the continental reversal chronology may be too coarsely dated to assign unique ages to individual marine anomalies
paleomagnetic samples may be contaminated by remagnetization, undermining the reversal sequence
sparse line crossings may aliasing the true anomaly pattern, producing apparent asymmetry unrelated to dynamics
magnetization variations in source rock could produce anomalies not tied to field reversals
fixed-crust advocates can add ad hoc paired-lithology structures to fit symmetric appearance, weakening statistical force
bet.generalizationBoundary: The result generalizes only to slow, roughly symmetric spreading along continuously surveyed ridge segments where the reversal chronology is independently established; it does not immediately constrain continental absolute motion, subduction-zone geometry, or fast/asymmetric spreading segments, nor does it resolve the mechanism question of mantle convection, so the discrimination claim is strictly kinematic and regional-to-global by extrapolation rather than direct proof.
unresolvedUnknowns: whether spreading rates have been constant enough for anomaly spacing to map linearly to time
whether ridge-created crust is magnetized exactly at the ridge axis or in a broad transition zone
whether separate ridge segments share a single global reversal clock
the fate of the subducting slab and whether it implies mass conservation requiring mantle return flow
whether continental paleomagnetic reversal dates can anchor marine anomaly ages within the needed precision
whether earthquakes at fracture zones indicate transform faulting or unrelated vertical tectonics

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is total launch mass versus a hard, finite Saturn launcher capability under a fixed decade deadline. Landing and returning from the Moon is physically impossible with existing vehicles in a single direct launch; the architecture must decide how to split mass (ascent stage, landing module, return spacecraft, propellant) across launches or lunar phases, so launcher throughput sets the entire program's feasibility envelope.

routes.route: choose direct ascent and develop a launcher large enough for the whole spacecraft
routes.reason: Direct ascent requires a launcher (Nova-class or beyond) that would consume unacceptable development schedule and budget given the finite Saturn family already in progress; the mass required to land the whole stack and lift off again is far beyond any near-term vehicle, and abort/recovery options degrade because the entire stack must commit to lunar landing.

routes.route: choose Earth-orbit rendezvous and assemble/refuel a larger lunar spacecraft in Earth orbit
routes.reason: Earth-orbit rendezvous relaxes launcher peak-mass but adds orbital assembly, transfer and refueling complexity, and it still launches a very large trans-lunar stack which imposes heavy landing and ascent mass once at the Moon. It is a serious rival but less mass-efficient than keeping a small module ashore, and its advantages depend on multi-launch reliability not yet demonstrated.

routes.route: choose lunar-orbit rendezvous with separate lunar and return spacecraft
routes.reason: LOR dramatically cuts the mass that must be landed and re-lifted off the Moon, keeping only a small lander/ascent stage on the surface while the command/service module loiters in lunar orbit. It leverages the finite Saturn V capability most effectively and keeps the return spacecraft shielded from landing risk, though it demands cislunar rendezvous and docking not yet routine.

routes.route: postpone architecture choice until a much larger launcher is demonstrated
routes.reason: Waiting for a larger launcher sacrifices scarce schedule on the fixed decade clock and has no guarantee such a vehicle will arrive; the existing Saturn family is the lever available now. Postponement converts a mass problem into a guaranteed deadline failure, and precursor missions can be flown while the architecture decision matures rather than stalling it.

routes.route: stage precursor rendezvous/navigation missions before committing crew to the full lunar landing sequence
routes.reason: Precursor uncrewed and early crewed rendezvous/navigation missions (Gemini-era docking practice, cislunar checkout flights) are the validation path that makes LOR's new rendezvous/docking risk acceptable. These stages are complements, not rivals: they de-risk the very capability LOR requires and should be paced in parallel with the Saturn V build.

bet.topRoute: choose lunar-orbit rendezvous with separate lunar and return spacecraft
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Conduct a full-system mass and launch budget analysis comparing direct-ascent, EOR, and LOR under the exact Saturn V payload limit, computing total launches, landed mass, ascent mass, and abort margins for each; then run a crewed Earth-orbit rendezvous/docking demonstration (extending existing Gemini-class docking capability) to prove cislunar rendezvous is achievable, which is LOR's one genuinely new and previously unvalidated risk.
